title: Incorporation Package for New NFPs
content:
# Incorporation Package for New NFPs

Source: https://www.masadvise.org/mas-publications/

Federal Not-for-Profit Incorporation via Corporations Canada
http://www.ic.gc.ca/eic/site/cd-dgc.nsf/eng/cs04970.html
Creating a Not-for-profit Corporation
Corporations under the Canada Not-for-profit Corporations Act (NFP Act) can be created (i.e., incorporated) by filing a request through Corporations Canada’s Online Filing Centre. If you prefer to submit a non-online request to create a corporation (i.e., by email attachment, fax or mail) this document will help you to prepare the request.
Note
The information provided is to assist you to complete the incorporation process quickly and accurately. It is not intended to replace legal advice. You may wish to consult a lawyer or other professional advisor to ensure that the specific needs of your not-for-profit corporation are met.
Table of Contents
* What documents must be filed to create a not-for-profit corporation?
* Related Information
* What do I need to do once the corporation has been created?
* Where can I find information on registering as a charity under the Income Tax Act?
* Is an NFP Act corporation automatically considered a non-profit organization under the Income Tax Act?
* Other Resources
What documents must be filed to create a not-for-profit corporation?
An application for a certificate of incorporation must include:
1. a completed and signed copy of Form 4001 – Articles of Incorporation (See available instructions) ;
2. a completed and signed copy of Form 4002 – Initial Registered Office Address and First Board of Directors (See available instructions) ;
3. a NUANS Name Search Report for the proposed name that is not more than 90 days old. If you have received prior approval of the name, attach a copy of the letter from Corporations Canada approving your name along with the copy of the NUANS Name Search Report. If the proposed name is a number name, a NUANS Name Search Report is not required; and
4. the filing fee.
The articles can be in English or French or in a bilingual format.
Professional Associations
Incorporation of a professional association (i.e., a corporation whose proposed name or purposes suggest that it considers itself to be an association of professionals) does not provide that corporation with the authority to practise, or to regulate the practice of, the profession. It is the corporation's responsibility to comply with provincial laws respecting professions.
Related Information
* How do I file my application?
* What happens after I submit my application?
What do I need to do once the corporation has been created?
Once the corporation has been created, a number of other items must be considered. Information on what needs to be done after a corporation has been created and on how to operate a not-for-profit corporation under the NFP Act is available on the Corporations Canada website.
By-laws
At the first organizational meeting, the directors may make by-laws. This process can be simplified by referring to theModel By-laws, which have been written to apply to a typical not-for-profit corporation.
Corporations Canada has also developed an online interactive tool called a By-law Builder that allows you to generate the by-laws you want by choosing provisions that meet the specific needs of your corporation from a number of available options.
Note
By-laws do not have to be filed with the application to obtain a Certificate of Incorporation. However, the NFP Act requires that they be filed within 12 months after the members have confirmed them.
Where can I find information on registering as a charity under theIncome Tax Act ?
To be able to issue official donation receipts and to be exempt from tax, the Income Tax Act requires that corporations created and operated exclusively for charitable purposes must register with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) as charities. The simple fact of being incorporated as a not-for-profit corporation under the NFP Act is not sufficient for a corporation to be considered either tax-exempt or a registered charity for the purposes of the Income Tax Act.
Information on charitable registration, along with the required application form, can be found on the CRA website or may be obtained by contacting:
Charities Directorate
Canada Revenue Agency
Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5
Toll Free: 1-800-267-2384
If your corporation intends to become a registered charity, CRA recommends that you submit a draft copy of Form 4001- Articles of Incorporation with your application to register as a charity and that your application to CRA be submitted prior to the time you file your application for incorporation. Otherwise, if CRA requires changes, the corporation may have to incur additional costs by applying to Corporations Canada for articles of amendment.
Is an NFP Act corporation automatically considered a non-profit organization under the Income Tax Act?
No. Incorporation under the NFP Act does not automatically mean that the corporation will be exempt from tax under the Income Tax Act. More information on non-profit organization under the Income Tax Act can be found on the CRAwebsite or by contacting CRA.
Other Resources
A number of other documents and tools are available to assist you in creating and operating a not-for-profit corporation:
* Model Form 4001 – Articles of Incorporation, which provides examples of wording that a typical not-for-profit corporation can refer to when completing its articles;
* Model by-laws, which provide examples of wording that a typical not-for-profit corporation can refer to when creating its by-laws;
* A By-law Builder, which is an online tool that will assist in creating by-laws; and
* A pamphlet, "Your Reporting Obligations under the Canada Not-for-profit Corporations Act", which describes the documents you are required to file with Corporations Canada.

title: Key Challenges Discussion Paper
content:
# Key Challenges Discussion Paper

Source: https://www.masadvise.org/mas-publications/

MANAGEMENT ADVISORY SERVICE 

Discussion Paper 

 

Pondering some new approaches to four key organization challenges identified by MAS Clients 

 

PART A: Background 

Management Advisory Service (MAS) is a small Toronto based charity that for 30 years has been recruiting highly skilled (mostly retired) executive and management level individuals and linking them up to provide free consulting to charities and not-for-profit organizations that come to us for help.  Over the years we have supported around 2,000 organizations complete strategic plans, learn about and develop their governance strategies, identify better processes in planning, finances, IT and fundraising, learn the basics of marketing and communication and grapple with human resource challenges, including volunteer engagement. 

Periodically we carry out a formal survey of the organizations we've helped in order assess our relevance to them, and to identify the areas where NFPs will need the most help moving forward.  Our 2024 survey results provide an interesting glimpse into the reality of the 255 organizations that sent in responses.  The following paper provides a very brief summary of top line results and a discussion on some of the key challenges identified by respondents. 

NOTES: 

For more information or a copy of the full survey report please contact MAS (info@masadvise.org). 

 

MAS is extraordinarily grateful for the help of David Saffran, a retired senior executive from the Angus Reid Institute and a most amazing MAS volunteer. David designed the MAS Client Survey, analyzed the results and wrote the final survey report(s). 

 

This summary and discussion document is written by Paddy Bowen, Executive Director of MAS.  Paddy has been a charity executive director for 35 years through leadership at Home Support Canada, Volunteer Canada, the Voluntary Sector Awareness Project and St. Felix Centre Toronto and has worked as an NFP program auditor, interim ED, consultant, presenter and writer in a broad range of organizations and topic areas.   

 

The discussion below (Part B) proffers the opinions of the author and do not reflect any formal position of MAS or the views of it's Members. 

 

The MAS Client Survey Respondents 

An online survey was sent September 2024 to 2,886 current and former MAS "clients" (charities and not-for-profits who have received pro bono consulting help over the past 10+ years).  

A total of N=255 completed survey responses were received. Six out of ten respondents were registered charities – the rest incorporated as not-for-profit organizations. 

The majority operate within the GTA and come from the following sub-sectors; education, social services, recreation/culture, healthcare and housing.  The majority identify a focus on support provided to marginalized populations. 

63% operate organizations with fewer than nine employees (53 of them having no paid staff at all).  In terms of financial status, a broad range is represented with 20% of respondents from organizations with annual funding under $50,000, 32% over $1M and the rest in between. 

A quarter of the organizations have been in existence for more than 15 years and 36% under five years. 

In summary, the respondents to the MAS Client survey reflect the usual – and wonderful - diversity of the Canadian charity/NFP sector.  They run the gamut of size from tiny to pretty big, (annual budgets over $3M) many operating with very few paid staff - although 30 of them reported having 50 or more paid employees.  Some are brand new while others have a long history of service.  Virtually all identified providing services to "marginalized" populations including low income, homeless, BIPOC, at-risk youth, seniors and children, people living with mental illness, disability or addictions, with a handful working in advocacy, policy or research. 

What they told us: their topmost challenges and priorities 

As below respondents identified their biggest challenge as funding, with recruiting and retaining volunteers (including Board members) as another. 

When asked to identify where they need consulting help, respondents' top choices were in the areas of fundraising and strategic planning.  

And in response to an invitation to comment on the critical issues, the following themes emerged from the hundred of comments provided: 

Fundraising/financing… There isn't enough, we need to know how to do it better (how to explain or promote our work), how to find Board or volunteers to fundraise.  No growth in government funding while operations are more expensive. Developing a sustainable funding model. Funders directing us and fund applications, processes and reporting very complicated/onerous… 

Volunteers: Loss of volunteers for a variety of reasons (age, post pandemic, interpersonal issues, increase in demand), we need more and "better" volunteers, we have issues keeping volunteers and this is different/more urgent than in the past.  The same applies to Board members – losing them, keeping them.  We need to clarify Board roles.  Challenges shifting from a hands-on, working Board to governance focused.  The difficulty of not achieving goals because of Board dynamics (opinions, hesitations) … 

Staffing: Senior staff retiring after a long time and so very difficult to replace.  Paying a decent wage, managing retirements, wages vs. inflation, managing difficult employees – making difficult decisions (not a skillset we have), managing a lot of different changes.  Having the right technology and the skills to use it… 

Growth: We want/need to grow but can't find the money.  There are more and more demands for our help as people struggle more financially/with addictions/with housing etc. etc.  Our strategic plan identifies growth as a goal. We need more money, more volunteers, better space if we are to grow… 

 

PART B: Discussion 

Issue #1: Funding   

The Challenge 

I don't really need to write very much here, do I?  There is not an organization in the charity and not-for-profit sector that does not have a need for more funding, pointe finale.  

I led a national consultation on voluntary sector issues in 2005 and the top concern of every one of the 1,500 charity organisations who participated, was funding.  I know for certain that nothing has changed in this regard over the past 20 years.  And the urgency around funding doesn't only apply to new or small entities trying to get a toehold in the sector.  Ask any hospital CEO if they need more funding and they will say yes… immediately. 

There are a few matters related to funding beyond the simplest one of there never being enough.  The issue of 'core funding' is relevant to a lot of organizations that live the reality of piecing together monies from funded projects or designated funds, in the absence of it.  The issue of sustainability hovers over many organizations who face uncertainty impacted by things like changes in government policy or downturns in the economy drying up donor funds.  Fundraising tactics are always evolving, as are questions of the capacity of organizations to simultaneously fundraise and deliver on their mission.  But overshadowing all of these is the ever-present concern for virtually every Board of Directors, senior leadership team, and development department; to find the necessary funds to achieve their respective goals. 

A Possible Response 

Pursuing funds will never not be a core activity of not-for-profit organizations and registered charities.  However, there is a common imperative in our sector which tends to focus on continuous growth – and not just growth that aligns with incremental increases related to cost of living, wages etc.  But growth in programs, services, scales of operation, bottom lines.  It is rare that a strategic plan is developed that doesn't identify goals related to 'doing more' or attracting more clients/support/donors/funders.  Operational planning and budgeting are often predicated on such expectations. 

My career as a charity executive was defined by the pressures that come with a desire for – an expectation of - continual growth.  It is only in my current state of semi-retirement and the work we do at MAS helping organizations struggling with the same kinds of stresses, that I have come to question why more, and bigger, are always considered to be better. 

And so, my suggested 'possible response' on matters related to funding, fundraising and growth, is more contrary than affirming.  I would challenge us to consider making the decision to plan operations based on the amount of funds we know we have on hand or can easily raise.  Living - if you will – within our means.   

But Paddy, many will say, demands for our services are growing… there are so many clients out there who need our help… we have to grow to stay relevant etc.  All true, and yet no matter how much larger your organization gets, the fact is there will always be more you could hypothetically do… more people you could serve.  No organization – unless legally mandated to provide universal services (such as hospitals, police services etc.) will ever cover the whole waterfront.  So, why not consider doing what you can, within the resources you have, and focus energy on delivering outstanding services vs. more of them?  Having pride and comfort saying, "this is how much we do and how many we serve"? 

Others have explored similar ideas around 'not growing', either out of pragmatism or in response to external factors.  The following few commentaries are only a scattershot of views on this.  I will leave these other wise commentators to conclude this brief discussion related to funding: 

 

"I feel we are making a huge mistake in aping the relentless desire for year-on-year growth in revenue, often - but not always - for its own sake. Many of us who work in the non-profit sector do so because we believe our organisations should be progressive ones that strive to set a higher bar. Most of the time we do so. However, I can't help but feel that our current obsession with growth is not only unsustainable, it's counter - progressive. We have in too many instances replaced being inspirational with being simply acquisitive. Why? Charities, under increasing pressure to 'run a tight business-like ship', increasingly (but not exclusively) appoint hawkish boards made up of businesspeople with a lifetime of growth-chasing under their belts. And so it goes on". 

"Have we developed an unnecessary obsession with growth in the non-profit sector?"   Toby Bourke, Global Director of Marketing, Communications and Fundraising, Hope and Homes for Children. LinkedIn, May 4, 2017 

 

 

"Survey findings have shown that charities are "scrambling to sustain growth" through diversified revenue strategies amidst economic challenges and increased service demands. However, while this shift demonstrates their resilience and innovation, the rise in business-like strategies could also divert focus from their core missions and strain resources".  

Charities Insights Canada Project, Nguyen, Thi Kim Quy, Postdoctoral Fellow, Carleton University, 2024 

 

"A charity requires clarity about what it is trying to achieve and how it will do that. Awareness of the things you are choosing not to do is as important as understanding what you are doing. This can help give the organisation focus and help it avoid getting distracted. You can't do everything. It is best to concentrate on what you can and do it to the best of your ability. Align the strategy with your charitable mission and resist any temptation to drift away from that". 

"Ten ways to ensure your charity is sustainable", Ian Allsop, Charity Digital.org.UK, January 2025 

 

"Unfortunately, most of the nonprofit sector's funding sources follow economic trends, meaning that when the country is facing economic troubles and demand for the sector's services rise, the sector has less resources than before to meet that demand. Government funding from all levels is one of the few counter-cyclical sources of sector funding, but whether governments will step in to fill funding gaps is an open question, especially at the federal level where there is so much uncertainty".  

What trends will impact charities and nonprofits in the first quarter of 2025? Emily Jensen,  Imagine Canada Blog post, February 5, 2025 

 

***** 

Issue #2: Volunteers 

The Challenge 

According to Volunteer Canada more than 65% of all charities and not-for-profit organizations have reported the same challenges recruiting and retaining volunteers as our small sample of agencies has.   

While young people have the highest rate of volunteering, their involvement tends to be sporadic (often one-time, related to education requirements or career goals).  Contrasting this, people over age 55 have a lower rate of volunteering but when they do, they contribute the highest number of hours of any cohort.   

It is no surprise to anyone in our sector that there is hardly an organization that hasn't benefitted from the contribution of a few (or if you're lucky quite a few) "super volunteers" from that group.  People who for years provide countless hours of time, are always ready to help in a variety of ways, whose presence and leadership essentially define the organization.  Unfortunately, these senior volunteers (both in terms of age and experience) are the people organizations are telling us we are losing.  So why have they dropped away?   

The major reason is they have other things to do.  This baby boom generation (currently age 57 to 77) are wedged between aging parents who are living longer than any generation before them, and their adult children facing job, housing, childcare and economic challenges that create greater dependence on their parents.   

As a 68-year-old baby boomer I know from personal experience how true this is.  I, like so many of my peers "left home" when I was 18.  My adult children lived with me into their late twenties.  My mother lived to be 96 and informal caregiving for her was also time consuming.  My personal picture is statistically replicated across my age cohort.   

Baby boomer aged volunteers are also healthier and wealthier than many previous generations.  As a result, they have busy and active lives engaged in travel, hobbies, sport and a myriad of late and post career activities.  Of course this doesn't describe every older volunteer; many don't fall into such an easy generalization. But whatever the reasons, older volunteers, traditionally the backbone of many volunteer programs, have quietly stepped away over the past five or so years, and organizations are feeling the impact.  

A last quick observation, which I'm not sure has been statistically proven yet, but from our survey respondents, and anecdotally in our work at MAS, we are told that when a lot of volunteer work moved into virtual modes during the COVID pandemic, many older people dropped away – and never came back.  Perhaps not liking the shift away from in-person or perhaps finding the time away providing a natural stopping point. 

A Possible Response 

Since my ten years at the helm of Volunteer Canada in the nineties/2000's I have been an advocate for strategic volunteer engagement and program design that does not depend on the contribution of 'super volunteers'.  Of course, if and when your organization has one or more of these wonderful people you will celebrate that enthusiastically (with and about them).   

But be aware – these are the volunteers who can burn out or just decide to leave - which is totally their right, of course - and you may find the hole where they were can seem pretty impossible to fill.   So, celebrate them yes, but avoid total dependence on them as individuals - or the general approach of expecting a lot from a very few. 

During the International Year of Volunteers (2001) at Volunteer Canada, we borrowed from the corporate sector and developed the use of 'Job Design' theory within volunteer programming.  Boiled down to its simplest explanation, this mean more consciously designing a volunteer program that offers a range of volunteer opportunities across a continuum of complexity and time consumption.   

The model challenges those who manage volunteer programs to not use the traditional 'one size fits all' approach to recruitment i.e. "Please come and be a volunteer with us – details on what you'll do and how much time will be involved will be worked out as we go along". 

The Job Design approach suggests that the "jobs" which are created should not all be the same and each one should be clearly outlined in a job description - which also delineates the term and weekly time commitment.  The range of ways to contribute are then varied; there are positions that require little time, or skills, while others need high or very specific skills and a great deal of time.  Or the opposite i.e. low skill/lots of time… high skill but few hours etc. 

This checkerboard approach offers people with less time to give, or who don't have a lot of work experience or specialized knowledge, choice in how they can get involved.  Good job descriptions are also a powerful recruitment tool making very clear what help (and how much) is needed.  And just as with paid positions they are a helpful and necessary management tool. 

Volunteer programs that recruit different kinds of people to fill different kinds of jobs are more robust and better able to withstand the natural ebb and flow of volunteer's participation. Most importantly they will better ensure the achievement of organizational missions and goals. 

A little case example: 

Like most temples, mosques, synagogues and churches, my family church in Ottawa ran a pretty traditional children's learning program – our Sunday School.  We are all familiar with the model; a handful (if you're lucky) of people agree to teach in the program for a number of months – generally over the school year – in a program which usually runs parallel to worship (often in the basement!).  As a result, those volunteers rarely get to attend services.  And over the years they have been harder and harder to recruit.   

I was asked to run the Sunday School at St. Bart's, and I decided to apply the Job Design theory I had been touting across Canada.  I stood up one September morning and said, "We need to recruit Sunday School teachers and we're using a slightly different approach; I'd like to ask you all to consider giving one or two Sundays between now and June…".   

Our program got a tremendous response.  No one wanted to take on the weekly commitment of teaching the kids, but doing one or two mornings?  No problem.  This being Rockliffe in Ottawa, we ended up with a Senator (parliamentary, not hockey!) a judge, a Member of Parliament and a handful of lawyers, doctors and some pretty great teens too.  Our children were exposed to a fascinating group of interesting and different adults, our program flourished, and people who would never have considered teaching in the Sunday School gladly gave the limited amount of time and effort required. 

 

***** 

Issue #3: Staffing 

The Challenge 

Based on our experience at MAS, and my own as a 35 years+ Executive Director, there are a myriad of challenges and issues facing charities and not-for-profit organizations when it comes to human resources and staffing.  Addressing them all would be a paper in an of itself and so at this juncture I will only comment on one matter that arose from our Client Survey. 

Many respondents provided feedback on their worry and frustration with not being able to pay adequate enough wages to properly compensate staff, and to address recruitment and retention issues.  The vast majority of community based NFPs have faced this reality and only the very largest, in the best resourced sub-sectors such as health care, tend to have wages that are competitive with other areas of the labour market. 

A Possible Response 

Notwithstanding the ever-present reality facing many charitable organisations in terms of inadequate funding, and not to in any way undermine valiant efforts to increase their funding bases, there is a way, in some instances, to allocate resources to allow for higher compensation rates without having to raise more money.  And it actually relates directly to the previous discussion on volunteer programming. 

The largest component of any NFPs budget is always salaries.  We are a sector of people who "do" things – we are service oriented vs. production.  I have worked in charities where the salary line is 95% of the total annual budget.  In most cases leadership in the organization have a lot of latitude on how they allocate those monies by position (unless there are funder constraints, or the environment is unionized in which case the strategy I am about to recommend would need to be discussed with those parties). 

Without going into a lot of detail (please feel free to contact MAS is you want more guidance though) one of the first steps in the Job Design methodology is an analysis of the full range of functions and tasks within the organization required to achieve the mission – without any consideration as to which work is paid for and which done by volunteers.   

At some point you will determine which element so the work you want or need to pay for (bearing in the mind that many organizations have only volunteer workers).  Normally, paid positions tend to encompass a broader range of tasks than volunteer ones – we would rarely hire someone to do just one thing while we may often engage a volunteer in a single-task job.  

The goal for any well-designed human resource plan is to use mission as the starting point for designing a matrix of jobs - paid and unpaid, full and/or part time etc. However, this is often not how it's actually done.   

Rather, the "real" work is seen to be done by paid people, while volunteer contributions are a nice 'add on'.  (Again, the exception to this being in those groups that have no paid people at all - where obviously everything is done by unpaid individuals).   

I confess that in my own time in planning and management – most often in mid size charities with paid staff cohorts - we rarely considered the volunteer element in terms of delivering on "essential" services.  The assumption was that work would be done – could only be done – by paid people.  (Kind of ironic considering my ten-year stint as the head of Volunteer Canada). 

But the fact is you can get a lot of impact – directly related to core service delivery – from a well-designed volunteer program.  More importantly, effective use of the volunteer element of human resources can give you a lot more creative wiggle room on how to allocate your financial resources for paid staff. 

When I was leading St. Felix Centre, a community-based place offering a range of services for homeless, low income, newcomer and marginalized folks in the downtown west core of Toronto, we had a rule.  Whenever we wanted to expand an existing program or develop a new one, our first question was never 'Can we find the money to hire someone to do this'.  It was 'Lets find the right volunteers to pull this off'.  I was also, in my role there as Executive Director, determined to lift the salaries of the small team of paid staff who worked alongside an amazing 700+ volunteers… 

St. Felix Centre had (still has I believe) a meal program.  When I started in 2008, they were serving around 7,000 meals a year and while there were volunteers involved in serving the meals (cafeteria style) very few were involved in the cooking or client related tasks, which were left to a few (very underpaid) staff i.e. one full time, two part time folks.   

Working with the long time and amazing kitchen manager and cook Iris, we identified a much more diverse set of roles for volunteers from ordering, picking up, storing, preparing food, to engaging with clients of the program, table service (a powerful way to connect with people not often served meals in this way), setting up, cleaning up, and more.  We decided to have only one paid person working in the program and guiding the volunteers.  From that point on Iris's job changed from being the cook, to being the supervisor, teacher and support for the teams of volunteers cooks we recruited.   

Fairly quickly (through attrition) the paid staffing allocation was one salaried position. Within six months we had brought on 300 new volunteers using all the elements of Job Design discussed above – planning, job descriptions etc. as well as a multi faceted shift schedule and a recruitment strategy that asked volunteers to sign on to at least one 3-hour shift a week.  We provided 20,000 meals that first year.  Just as importantly I was able to double the salary of the program manager. 

A final thought on paying for higher salaries: 

My personal philosophy has always been to operate within a sufficiency mindset ie. There is THIS much money available… THIS is our mission… HERE is how we can use those monies toward achieving that mission…  

So, whatever the bottom-line amount of dollars in the budget is, and within a variety of constraints such as Board guidance/approval, funding contracts, existing commitments etc., my goal is always to allocate those monies as creatively as possible, while staying laser focused on the core mission/desired outcome.  I should note that I have applied this approach in organizations ranging in budget size from $50K a year to $7.5M. 

I am not advocating for a replication of my personal approach but am rather adjuring readers of this essay to think outside the proverbial box when it comes to the allocation of funds to human resources.   

Have fewer paid people… pay them more… fill the gaps with volunteers, cleverly designing your volunteer program to be always renewing and never asking too much of any one individua).  

You likely won't stop wanting to bring in more funding as discussed above, and you will need to work with paid staff to change their mindset in terms of working alongside volunteers as peers, but this ultimately simple approach, depending on your unique context, is one you may wish to consider to address the challenge of paying your people more, and more competitively. 

 

***** 

 

 

 

Issue #4: Strategic Planning 

The Challenge 

Requests for help with strategic planning is MAS's most common request.  Our volunteer consultants carry out around 150 strategic plan projects every year. From very large, to very small or new organizations, there is a pervasive sense that they must have a strategic plan. 

In much of my experience as an Executive Director, starting in the late eighties, I didn't really encounter strategic planning.  Not until the 2000's certainly.  It just wasn't a common practice and I'm not totally sure where the avid desire to engage in formal strategic planning came from - vs. good operational planning and Board governance planning, both of which have always been an element of NFP work. 

It seems to me that the 2000's brought a trend into charity work that shifted us to more corporate modes of operating.  Others more learned than me in these things could address this better.  But there is no doubt that along with things like outcome measurement, logic models, and accrual accounting, Strategic Plans became a fixture and, in some cases, a significant burden for Boards and senior staff both.   

I have been told many stories of super costly strategic planning processes – up to $50,000 – even in only mid sized organizations.  I have been told of Strategic Plans that get drawn up and then are literally never looked at again.  I have seen firsthand Boards, early in their formation, still struggling with the basics of governance, trying to establish strategic directions long before their organization is ready. 

A possible response 

While I would not advocate eliminating the use of strategic plans – if nothing else the shared exercise that staff and volunteers and Board embark on in the process can have really positive impacts on cohesion and commitment – I certainly think they can be significantly simplified.  

I personally recommend to many organizations that they create a 'one page' strategic plan that articulates a vision, a mission and three to four high level goals for the 'what' the organization seeks to achieve over the next three years.  A secondary annual operational plan will complement this by providing details on 'how'. 

I also have a personal bugaboo about strategic plans which almost always identify strategies for growing… doing "more" etc. (As discussed above in Funding).  Why is it not ok to have a strategic goal for "doing what we do now, really really well for the next few years"?  Do the strategies always have to lay out something new?  Personally, I don't think so. 

I am not alone in my view that the time has come for a serious re-think about strategic planning in the not-for-profit world.  The thoughts below are only a smattering of what others are beginning to think and write.  I'll leave them to further challenge readers on this pervasive and timely topic.  And moving forward I would strongly recommend a discussion at Board tables, and further reading and research, to identify and discuss the future approach of your organization when it comes to strategic planning.   

"There has been a growing acknowledgment that the realities and issues facing the nonprofit community are ever-changing and evolving from year to year, presenting questions about the efficacy of the traditional 3–5-year strategic planning process".  

 The Revolution of Nonprofit Strategic Planning: Fusing Tradition with Innovation, Jaron Bernstein, MBA, Alford Group, August 2024 

 

"BoardSource has also seen a shift away from traditional strategic plans based on three- to five-year time horizons and long planning processes. There has been a move toward strategic frameworks articulating organizational priorities, business plans that combine programmatic and operational goals with financial forecasts, as well as more robust annual plans with clear metrics and timelines".  

Board Source: Resources for Nonprofit Boards; "Nonprofit Strategy and Planning" 2024 

 

"This practice of taking significant time off to determine your strategies and priorities is not only extremely aggravating, but it's also steeped in privilege and is harmful to not only the nonprofits that rely on you for funding, but to the people who rely on the nonprofits."  

Nonprofit AF newsletter, Vu Le, 2023 

 

"When you should not develop a new nonprofit strategic plan: 

When there is a lack of stability at your nonprofit 

When there is a lack of resources (financial, human) 

When the organization is having an identity crisis 

When external factors are dominating the landscape 

In these instances, we advocate for shorter-term planning that focuses on helping nonprofits identify two to three priorities or things that need to be accomplished over the next six months or one year". 

Prosper Strategies, Lindsay Mullen, September 2023 

 

"It's time for some truth-telling. The nonprofit sector has created a culture in which strategic work is seen as a necessary evil, a process to endure, something to suffer through…. When it comes to strategic planning, chief executives often feel sure they know the right answer and already have a sense of what needs to get done in the next few years. Board members will tell you their voices aren't heard or valued. Precious few board members find making plans invigorating or enriching, nor are they excited to promote a new strategy to potential donors".  

Strategic Planning Sucks the Life Out of Nonprofits, Joan Garry (First published in the Chronicle of Philanthropy on Oct 23, 2019) 

 

***** 

In Conclusion 

I will not engage in my university essay requirements of concluding with a summary of the above discussion.  Suffice to say I hope some of these ideas may resonate with readers.  If you have any questions or comments, please don't hesitate to reach out me through MAS.  Also, please do not hesitate to contact MAS if we can be of any help on these, or other issues where you may need consulting help, or if there are matters raised in these pages that you would like to discuss. 

 

Paddy Bowen 

March, 2025

expect? 

1.  Clarify your messages and make a great website 
2.  Copy from your website to create all other promotional items 
3.  Once a year, audit yourself. 

Copywriting - The ability to write clearly and succinctly. 

Basic tech skills – Building a website on WordPress.com is as 
easy as Powerpoint.  It is different, but just as easy.  If you are not 
a wiz at Powerpoint, find someone who is and they can quickly 
learn Wordpress.com. (Avoid WordPress.org which is the front 
end designed for coders who understand HTML.) 

Outside, fresh eyes – If you are distracted by day-to-day crises, it 
is hard to see yourself like a donor or new volunteer sees you.

Why MAS 
made this 
booklet? 

This booklet is the minimum you need to get started.   
Marketing done badly is easy to do;  marketing done well is hard. 
This booklet will help your nonprofit look professional so that you 
can attract donors and volunteers. 

2 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 #1 Describe in <50 words your who/what/where/when/why/how 

What is your elevator speech?  Eg. “MAS is a pro bono consulting 
service operating in Toronto since 1993.  As a volunteer-run charity, 
we help nonprofits in governance, strategy, HR, marketing and 
fundraising.  Our 50+ Volunteer Consultants are professionals who 
give back using the skills we learned in our careers.”  
!   Place on your main webpage. 

#2 Why are you unique? 

Why do you deserve a donation (vs the thousands of other charities 
in Canada)?  Why should donors care about your cause?  Why is 
your charity a good way to address the cause?  What would happen 
if you did not exist?  Would recipients do without?  Would they 
have to travel further for help? 
! Place on a “Why we are unique” webpage 

#3 What is your track record? 

What is the amount of good you do?  What did you accomplish last 
year?  Prove to donors you are worthy of a donation. 
!    Place all external metrics on an “Our impact 2017” webpage 

#4 What impact will a donation have? 

Describe examples based on your average donation price points, eg 
$20 pays for a bug net, $200 pays for counseling.  Set the first price 
point above your average donation to “anchor” the donor’s 
decision.  Consider giving “social proof” such as “most donors give 
$60” to help donors choose an amount.  Include a stretch donation.  
!    Place on Donate webpage 

#5 What do you need more of? 

Do you need more volunteers?  Revenue?  Recipients? Awareness 
of cause? Awareness of your nonprofit?  Members? Gifts-in-kind?  
Now, put your needs in priority.

your 
messages

Remember: before you tell a donor HOW to donate, you must convince them 
WHY to donate.   
•  What happens if you did not exist, “Without us, our clients …”

your donation can make, cost efficient, if you want to help we are the best 
way to attain your wish.   

•  Key words for belonging donors:  pay it forward, give back, prevent, your 

donation is you where you cannot be. 

•  Key words for imagination donors: imagine a time without, envisage a 

better future for, just think, if only, what if. 

•  Why immediate need? “You can shorten our waiting list...”

caution

 … if you are lucky. 
•  Do dropdown boxes sufficiently describe the work you do? 
•  Navigate from every page to every page?

they need? 

Visitors will spend 8 seconds on a webpage 
Most viewers will spend only 8 seconds, which means they read 
30 words. Select a few words to highlight in bold. Be ruthless 
about removing clutter – ensure a viewer’s eyes will be drawn to 
where you want them to look. 

Spend more time on your website than your annual report  
Everything should be on your website so that everyone can learn 
about you, all year round.  When you need to make your annual 
report, copy from your website.   

Problems with marketing projects are rarely about 
marketing.  Although the symptoms may appear to be 
marketing, they are typically caused by deeper issues with 
governance or HR.  If your governance structure is not well 
defined, it is hard to create an external face.  If your HR policies 
create tension, it will be hard to reach consensus.   
Fix your other problems, before starting on marketing. 

Top 5 
1.  Great menu  

•  Drop down boxes self-explain the work you do 
•  Placeholders (so the first content  page shows in the drop down box) 
•  Every page is accessible from every page 

2.  Great home page 

•  Explain who/what/where/when/why/how 

3.  Easy-to-read back pages 

•  Short text - short words - short sentences – short paragraphs.         

Aim for a comprehension level of grade 9.  

•  Lots of subtitles to make it easier to scan 
•  Lots of bullet points (or numbered lists) 
•  Bold key words (avoid italics and colours) 
•  Add one photo per page and wrap text around it. 
•  At the bottom, state what the viewer should do or who to call 

4.  Stories (maximum 100 words) 
5.  Real photos (not stock)	

5 

 
 
 
 
 
 Build your 
own 
brochure 

Draw a mockup  
•  Fold an 8x11 sheet twice.  Brochures have 6 panels.  Two 

panels are the front and back cover.  Four panels are for text 
and photos. If your text can be split evenly, fold into a Z-fold 
(2 panels each side, see below) Copy and paste from your 
website to ensure consistency. 

•  Always leave a white border around the edges so that the 

white margin left by your printer won’t be obvious. 

•  Do not include: mission/vision, stories (print separately on 
letterhead), impact (print separate updatable infographic).   

Watch this great how-to video

Assume a 10 minute presentation (30 seconds per slide): 
Slide 1 – title and logo (ensure look is consistent with website) 
Slide 2 – elevator speech from Main webpage 
Slide 3 – summarize Services webpages 
Slide 4 – “Why we are Unique” webpage 
Slide 5 – “Our impact” last year webpage 
Slide 6 – about me (your own story of why you love your cause) 
Slide 7 - Learning objectives for today  
Slides 8-18 – facts, photos and stories about your cause 
Slide 19 – Get involved (what you want donors to do) 
Slide 20 – Thank you. Questions (add logo and contact info)  6 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
	
	
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
	
	
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 TIPS to improve your ranking in search engines 

1.  A website that is easy for humans to read, is easy for search engines to read. 

•  Easy-to-find answers to donor questions 
•  No clutter  

2.  Key words 

•  No jargon, use words that real people search for 
•  Place key words in subheads and tags 

3.  Backlinks from reputable websites (with no corresponding outbound link from you) 
4.  Good quality, fresh readable content - original text. your own photos (correctly-tagged), videos. 

•  Short words and short sentences. 

5.  Traffic 

•  Replace PDFs with content on webpages.  In emails, link to your webpages 
•  Link website to your social media 
•  Refresh your website theme every 3 years   

TIPS to write great stories 

•  Do your stories explain 50% before and 50% after?  Donors can find it too disturbing to hear 

about life before; they want to hear about life after because they want to see the difference their 
donation made.  Although your clients may be more articulate about their life before, their 
gratitude for their life after may be too emotional for them to reveal. It’s a balance. 
•  Do you have a pipeline from your frontline staff about clients with potential stories?  
•  Max 100 words.  Use bold and subheads to make it easier for readers to scan quickly. 
•  Wide range of topics (day-in-the-life client, about a donor, this-day-10-years-ago, about an 

employee, about a volunteer) 

Annual marketing audit 

Lay out  all your promotional items on a table.  This includes everything that shows your logo: 
business cards, annual report, letterhead, brochures, posters. 
Ask yourself: 
•  Is the overall look consistent? (colours, design) 
•  Are the messages consistent?  Is your elevator speech consistent? 
•  Is the text succinct? 
•  Do the photos convey the message? Compelling emotion? 
•  Can an outsider understand the message if they scan an item for 2 seconds? (Are subheads and 

bold sufficient?) 

•  Is the call-to-action obvious?  Are there various calls-to-action to allow for different levels of 

engagement? (email signup vs attend event) 

•  Enews – is it a struggle to create fresh content?  Is it educational and newsworthy or self-flattery 

and donation requests? 

Review the analytics of your website 
•  Which webpages get the most traffic? 
•  Which webpages get the longest time-on-page? 

7 

	
 TIPS for great videos

•  Key points explained in first 10 seconds 
•  Subtitles (for silent viewing)

title: Marketing Research for MAS Clients

# Marketing Research for MAS Clients

Source: https://www.masadvise.org/mas-publications/

Application of Marketing Research for Non-Profit Organizations

Tim Hodapp

Senior staff at non-profit organizations are challenged on a regular basis to make critical, cost-effective decisions.  Marketing research – the process of systematically gathering and analyzing decision-critical information about citizen/service user wants, needs, beliefs and behaviour – can assist in this effort.  While conducting marketing research activities may require some cost to the organization, this can be a worthwhile investment if it leads to more effective, fact-based decisions.

Marketing research is applied under two broad categories of work.  Strategic applications impact the overall direction of an organization.  Tactical research consists of planning, developing and implementing the actual activities for delivering your services to the market. Strategic research supports the idea. Tactical research supports the action.

Specific applications of marketing research for non-profits and typical questions they can answer include, but are not limited to:

Strategic

Organizational/service awareness, usage and attitudes:  What are the levels of awareness and use of the organization and its specific services among the general population or specific target groups?  What opinions do people have of the organization and its services?  Have recent communications and other initiatives had an impact on awareness, usage and opinions?  

Market/user segmentation: What are the demographic, psychographic, motivational, cultural and behavioural characteristics of potential/actual service users?  What communications strategy would resonate best with key target groups?

User decision-making:  What is the relative importance of the various factors that motivate people to use a program or service?  What is the process used to decide on whether to use a program/service or not?

Tactical

Communications:  How well are specific communications initiatives meeting objectives for building awareness, image and use?  Is the format working effectively?  Is the content too complex or not detailed enough?

Program/service:  To what extent is your program/service meeting user needs and expectations?  Where can improvements be made?  

Pricing: If a charge is applied for program/service use, what features are most valuable to potential users and how much are they willing to pay for them.  What is the most basic service that can be offered for the lowest price?  What other aspects can be offered as optional add-ons?

User satisfaction/experience/loyalty:  Are program/service users satisfied with the overall experience as well as with each of the touchpoints included in using a given program/service? Are users likely to continue with the program/service or will they look for another provider or stop altogether? 

Mystery usage:  Is the program or service being delivered as intended?  Is training needed to ensure compliance by service providers with stated standards.

Two main sources of data are generally used for marketing research. Primary research is customized to meet specific information needs with targeted data collected to address the problem/question at hand. Secondary research sources publicly accessible data that has been collected for other purposes. Secondary research generally costs far less than primary research, but seldom comes in a form that exactly meets the needs of the researcher.

Two main methods are used for primary research.  Qualitative research is generally used for exploratory purposes, producing results not generalizable to the whole population.  Examples include focus groups, in-depth interviews and projective techniques.  Quantitative research allows for conclusions to be made with a given level of confidence from results gained through systematic surveys among relatively large samples of a target population.  

Certainly, marketing research has its limitations.  It is not an exact science, even though it uses the techniques of science.  The results of any research project are only as good as the people who manage the collection, analysis and reporting of data and the staff who apply the findings and insights to their organization.

As you may know, MAS’ mandate is limited to advising clients on problems or issues of importance.  The client is responsible for implementing or operationalizing the actions resulting from that consulting activity with MAS.  For marketing research activities, a MAS volunteer consultant would serve as the in-house research manager for the client.  We would, in consultation with the client:

Develop the objectives and scope of the project

Design the project specifications and methodology

Prepare a Request for Information (RFI) or Request for Proposal (RFP) to be sent to potential vendors

Assist in the review of RFI/RFP responses and the selection of vendors as needed

Review any questionnaires (for quantitative research) or discussion guides (for qualitative research) prepared by the selected vendor

Monitor the work of the vendor in terms of sample selection, data collection, data analysis, report/presentation preparation

Facilitate action-planning workshops based on project results.

Aspects of a research project that may incur costs for the client include:

Purchase of names of potential study respondents (sample)

Recruitment and incentive fees for respondents

Rental of facilities, if needed, for qualitative sessions or for quantitative in-person interviews.

Contracting with a third-party researcher for such activities as questionnaire development, data collection, data analysis, report/presentation preparation.

title: Marketing Self-Audit for Mid-sized Charities
content:
# Marketing Self-Audit for Mid-sized Charities

Source: https://www.masadvise.org/mas-publications/

Mid-size 
Nonprofits: 
Marketing 
Self-audit 

www.masadvise.org 
info@masadvise.org 
416-963-5792 
November 2018 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Definition of a mid-size nonprofit? 

This audit applies to your nonprofit if you: 
•  claim over $100,000/year to the CRA for fundraising expenses? 
•  have 1+ staff on marketing or fundraising? 
•  have a donor database? 

If you claim less than $100,000/year, only some audit questions will apply 
to you (questions 1,2,10,11,12,13). 

If you claim significantly more, the same 15 audit questions apply to you. 
However, your answers will be more complex.   

Surprisingly, revenue is not a predictor of marketing complexity (because 
of large or fluctuating in-kind donations and government grants.) 

Why do a marketing audit? 

1.  To examine marketing efforts to ensure efficiency and identify gaps. 

2.  As preparation for your Strategic Planning review, a marketing audit will 

identify marketing SWOTs and action plans. 

3.  To select marketing metrics to show to the Board annually.   

What are the risks? 

A marketing audit can: 

•  uncover non-marketing issues.  Marketing problems are rarely caused by 

marketing.  If they were, marketers could fix them. Instead, many marketing 
problems are symptoms of deeper problems, usually in HR or governance.  For 
example, a charity in decline because of Founder’s Syndrome;  a federated 
charity model where roles are unclear; a toxic work culture; difficult 
employees.  It may be a better use of your time to fix your foundational 
problems first.   

•  produce a range of emotion.  Audits are scary.  Some employees will be open 
(new hires or lateral transfers from operations for career development).  Long 
term employees will worry how the audit reflects on them.   

2			

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 Marketing Self-audit 

The Art of Marketing  
#1 Is your brand clear, concise and consistent? 
#2 Does the time staff spend on activities reflect your non-profit’s priorities? 
#3 Does the marketing department have a culture of creative experimentation? 
#4 Do you have a range of acquisition and retention activities per donor type? 
#5 Have you reviewed the risks to your brand? 

The People of Marketing 
#6 Do you have a combination of marketing generalists and specialists? 
#7 How is marketing’s interaction with other departments? 
#8 How do you offer professional development? 
#9 How do you ensure your marketers thrive? 

The Science of Marketing 
#10 Do you track which are your most cost-effective revenue sources? 
#11 Do you track how concentrated each revenue source is? 
#12 Do you track the churn in your donor portfolio? 
#13 Do you connect marketing results to your marketing activities? 
#14 Have you customized your own nonprofit’s Rules of Thumb? 
#15 Membership-based nonprofits: additional analysis for you. 

Tips for the ED 
Tips for the Project Manager 

Why MAS made this booklet 

As a pro bono consulting charity, our mission is to build capacity. We want to 
help mid-size nonprofits do better marketing. This self-audit will answer: 

Marketing staff: “How can we work smarter?” 
ED: “How can I measure the effectiveness of our marketing?” 
Board members: “What are the marketing questions I should ask?” 
Consultants: “How can I add value?” 

3			

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 The Art of Marketing 

#1 - Is your brand clear, concise and consistent? 

Clear website? 
•  Does your main webpage answer who/what/where/when/why? 
•  Do you have pages that address the 3 donor questions?  (Why should I donate to 
you? What was your impact last year? What will my donation buy, at different 
price points?) 

•  Does your navigation bar self-explain the work you do? 
•  How transparent is your website? (PDF financial reports, staff names, CRA#) 
•  Does your website portray the look you want? (established, youthful, caring) 

Concise website? 
•  Can each page be understood in 8 seconds (lots of subheads, bolds, bullets) 
•  Does each page have a Readability Score at grade 9 level? 

Are marketing tools consistent with website?  
•  Are the key messages in the text consistent across all marketing tools? 
•  Are the visuals consistent? Do you have a Brand Guide on fonts/colours? 
•  How do you ensure consistency between departments? 

#2 – Does the time staff spend on activities reflect your 
nonprofit’s priorities? 

•  What does your nonprofit want more of? (donations, in-kind donations, volunteers, 
recipients, supporters, awareness of nonprofit, awareness of your cause)  Is this 
priority reflected in your website navigation bar and all marketing tools? 

•  How do you track your marketing staff time (eg fundraising, mission, admin?) 
•  Can you track marketing staff time spent by donor type? 
•  Does your website receive the appropriate time and creative energy (vs annual 

reports and newsletters)? 

•  Is the time staff spend on social media/blog/content creation appropriate given 

your nonprofit’s priority for awareness.   

•  What ratio of time is spent on creating content vs posting/tracking/analyzing? 

(80:20 seems to be typical) 

•  How do you balance program/advocacy messages with fundraising appeals? 
•  Do you have a pipeline that generates ideas for stories for publications? 

4			

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   The Art of Marketing 

#3 - Does the marketing department have a culture of creative 
experimentation? 

•  Is there an expectation to test every year a certain number of new ideas for marketing activities?  
•  Do you run concurrent tests on your direct mail? (eg A/B testing) 
•  Do you summarize conclusions in a final report (to add to institutional memory)? 
•  What are the emotional and career consequences to failure? 
•  Is there a culture of experimentation in the rest of the nonprofit? 

#4 – Do you have a range of acquisition and retention activities 
per donor type? 

•  Do you have a formal process to select new marketing activities, eg cost/benefit? 
•  What is the optimal number of solicitations and retention messages before donor fatigue starts? 
•  Have you reviewed from a donor’s point of view, every point of contact they have with you? All 
contacts, not just fundraising appeals.  Make flow charts of touch points for each donor type. 
Here are examples for 3 donor types.  The white boxes are existing activities; orange boxes are 
upcoming experiments; lapsed donors are included in each.  You will need these flow charts for 
Question #12 where you will find that some donor types need more orange boxes under 
acquisition, other donor types need more retention orange boxes. 

•  Do staff regularly make small donations to test the journey and ensure messages are consistent, 

messages are personal, welcome emails sent immediately, unnecessary steps removed?  

5			

 
 
 
 
 The Art of Marketing 

#5 – Have you reviewed the risks to your brand? 

Risks that become public 
•  Have you reviewed external risks (your name is confused with others; another 

nonprofit has poor publicity)? 

•  Have your reviewed internal risks (employee fraud, board member conflict of 

interest)? 

•  Do you have a PR emergency plan? 
•  Have you reviewed and learned from how staff handled a recent crisis? 
•  How complete is your orientation for employees handing social media? 
•  Do you track donor complaints? 
•  Do you have enough spokespeople with media training? 

Risks of employee decisions 
•  Decision making (decisions made in a hurry, new employees who want to 

make their mark, employees who don’t want to change) 

•  Have you built institutional memory (documented touch points per donor 

type, results of marketing experiments, Brand Guide) 

Financial risks 
•  Do you have diversity of revenue sources (see question #10) 
•  Do you have diversity within each revenue source (see question #11) 

Regional chapter risks 
•  Does the national office act as a gatekeeper for communicating with donors? 
•  Are roles clear? Are approval procedures clear? 

6	

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 The People of Marketing 

#6 - Do you have a combination of marketing generalists 
and specialists? 

•  Strategy – messaging, budgeting, inter-department dynamics 
•  Financial analyst – cost effectiveness of revenue sources, donor churn 
•  Writers - produce newsletters, write stories 
•  Graphic designers – annual report, marketing tools 
•  Social media – promote events, manage website 
•  Public relations - create awareness of cause, AGM, press releases, PSAs 
•  Database – update donor data, tax receipts, produce management reports 
•  Fundraisers – research prospects, staff with assigned portfolios 

There are risks to combining roles. The skills are different: some are creative, some 
analytical.  Fundraising and public relations need people skills.   

#7 – How is marketing’s interaction with other 
departments? 

Fundraising 
•  Is there a balance of power between marketing and fundraising? 
•  How would you rate cooperation and trust between staff? 
•  Are marketing staff able to interact directly with major donors and corporations? 

Operations  
•  Is marketing regularly embedded in operations?   
•  Is time in operations included in marketing staff orientation? 
•  Do marketing staff attend other department meetings? 
•  Does marketing offer show’n’tells to other staff? 
•  Does marketing staff offer brand training to other teams?  

Senior team 
•  Do marketing staff get enough attention or the information they need to do their job? 
•  Do the senior team understand how long projects take?  Your typical day? 

Board 
•  Do you need a Marketing Committee of volunteers and Board members? 

Federated charity model 
•  How aligned are the marketing priorities between head office and regions? 
•  Are HR issues getting in the way of resolving marketing conflicts? 
•  Do you think like a collection of mid-size nonprofits or do you combine your 

strengths and think like a large nonprofit? 

7			

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 The People of Marketing 

#8 – How do you offer professional development? 

Formal 
•  Do you have a budget to attend conferences and workshops? 
•  If no, do your staff attend on their own time? 

Informal 
•  Do marketing staff have internal/external peers with whom they can share ideas? 
•  Where do staff get inspiration from to improve marketing practices? (eg other 

nonprofits inside your cause, outside of your cause) 

•  How do your marketing staff grow in a mid-size organization? (vs large 
organizations that can offer lateral transfers between product lines) 

#9 – How do you ensure your marketers thrive? 

•  Does marketing staff have a quiet time each year for long term planning? 
•  How do you balance planned activities with ad hoc requests? 
•  Do your marketing staff have annual targets?   

•  specific to tasks (# newsletters, social media) 
•  general target for total fundraising revenue 
• 

target specific to donor type (eg revenue from regular donors) 

•  Do you have an orientation plan for new marketing staff? 
•  What is the typical career path for marketing staff? 
•  Have you thought about succession planning in the short term and long term? 
•  What are the top frustrations marketing staff have? 

8			

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 The Science of Marketing 

#10 – Do you track which are your most cost-effective 
revenue sources? 

Calculate the Revenue Efficiency Report (page 16) and discuss the results: 
•  Which are the most cost-effective revenue sources? 
•  Do some of the revenue sources that are cost-effective at the front end, have higher 
back-end costs, and are therefore not as desirable? (eg reporting government grants) 

•  Are you satisfied with the diversity of your revenue sources? 
•  Are there more risks associated with some revenue sources? 
•  Where do similar nonprofits obtain their revenue? 
•  Which revenue source has the most room to grow? 
•  Which revenue sources are more constant vs volatile? Predictable vs unpredictable? 
•  Do you have the right balance between cost efficiency vs other goals? (eg activities that 
raise general awareness, communications on mission, fundraising events that also thank 
volunteers, fundraising events that are more “friendraisers” in the long term) 

•  Is the allocation of staff time appropriate? 
•  What is your definition of a major gift? Is the $1,000 threshold appropriate or should 

you lower it (eg to $500) to give more donors individual attention? 

•  Do some donors have a higher “lifetime value”, eg monthly donors with automatic 

withdrawals vs annual donors where it is easier to not renew?  How does the tenure of a 
donor on your database compare to the industry average of 1 year 9 months. 
•  Are you  more successful asking corporations to donate (eg employee matching 

program) or to sponsor (eg logo to increase their profile)? 

#11 Do you track how concentrated each revenue source is? 

Calculate the chart (page 17) and identify: 
•  How exposed you are if one donor in each revenue source did not renew. 

#12 - Do you track the churn in your donor portfolio? 

Calculate the Donor Churn Report (page 18) and discuss: 
•  Are you better at acquiring or retaining donors in each revenue source? 
•  Which revenue sources are more loyal? (Compare renewal ratios. For regular donors, a 
renewal ratio over 40% is good.  For major donors, a renewal ratio over 80% is good.) 

•  Review any gaps in the touch points within each revenue source (question #4) to 

identify any marketing experiments you can test. 

9			

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 The Science of Marketing 

#13 - Do you connect marketing results to your marketing 
activities? 

Complete the chart (page 19) after discussing: 
•  Can you re-align staff time to improve cost-efficiency of each revenue source? 
•  Can you re-align staff projects to address gaps in acquisition or retention? 
•  Can you compare year-over-year to show impact of previous marketing experiments? 
•  Can you compare year-over-year to identify real trends vs noise in your data vs random 

donor behaviour? 

#14 – Have you customized your own non-profit’s Rules of 
Thumb? 

Complete the chart on page 20. 

Consider setting up procedures to track your own ratios.  Why? 
•  your staff can get better at predicting revenues.  
•  Educate your colleagues and Board members - some revenue sources take longer to gear 

up 

•  add to your nonprofit’s institutional memory for new employees.   

#15 – Membership nonprofits – additional analysis for you 

Most of the questions above apply to you (except #10,11,13).  Here are additional idea: 

•  Activation of members 
In addition to measuring acquisition and retention of members (similar to charity’s donors), 
you also measure activating your members.  You need to measure popularity of your 
activities, partner discounts and partner benefits.  Membership surveys are critical.   

•  Market share 
You know how many potential members qualify, you can track your share over time. 

•  Rich data allows you to perform deeper predictive modeling 

•  Pricing membership 
In addition to pricing annual fees, you can experiment with pricing individual activities.  
Offering discounts can be tricky. 

Check out the 4 minute video that provides templates for reports customized to your needs 
at (www.MasAdvise.org/ marketing mid-size). 

10			

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Tips for the ED 

Select a project manager 
This self-audit is written for anyone with a business degree.  Because of the “case study” 
approach to learning, business students learn theory from the textbook and apply the theory 
using a case study.  Here, this self-audit is the theory, your nonprofit is the case.  As well, 
the section on Science requires a basic understanding of cost accounting.   

Select an employee who understands your entire organization, is comfortable crunching 
numbers and has an open mind.  Pick from anywhere in your organization.  Not necessarily 
from your Fundraising department (who may have vested interests in the results).  Nor from 
your Marketing department (who may be more creative than analytical). Consider an up-
and-coming employee who deserves an introduction to senior management.   

Other options: 
•  Ask a board member on your Fundraising Committee 
•  MAS - pro bono consultants available by Skype.  We can coach your project manager or 

be your project manager.    

Free up staff time 
Project Manager – Expect 20 hours over the course of 8 weeks for meetings and writing the 
final report.  Monitor your project manager’s time.  It is enticing to spend too much time on 
these reports; stop when they reach a point where more information will not alter a decision.   

The Art: 3 hours each for Project Manager and marketing staff 
The People: 3 hours each for Project Manager and ED/Marketing VP 
The Science: 6 hours each for Project Manager, database staff and ED/Marketing VP for 
          meetings. Database staff will require 10 more hours for data retrieval.  Since these 
          reports should be produced every fiscal year end, next time the reports will be 
          faster to produce. You will be looking at data in a new way and you may not have all 
          the data. Treat this year as a trial run.  Set up procedures to track more thoroughly, so 
          next year’s reports will be more accurate.  

Expect resistance 
Find a way to protect your project manager from employees who will create resistance: 
• 
•  senior level fundraisers who may feel threatened by making their results more transparent 
•  employees who are motivated by your cause and resist attempts at a business approach 

long term employees who have done marketing and fundraising in the past 

Tips 
•  Review the efficiency of all revenue sources, not just the sources that marketing focuses 

on (eg regular donors). This creates an attitude that you are not singling out a department. 

•  Be careful who you show the results to. It is possible that the reports can identify poor 

performing employees.  

11			

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Tips for the Project Manager 

How do I start? 
Send the list of audit questions (see MAS website for free one page summary) to each 
participant.  Book an initial 2 hour meeting with each. Start with the section on 
Science, it takes the longest to complete.  

Your role is to judge process, not content 
The questions are phrased to estimate the quality and time staff have spent on topics. 
It is not your role to debate individual points.   For example, when evaluating risks in 
question #5, you need to measure preparedness.  If your colleague has thought a lot 
about risks and handled one recently – assign a great rating.  If your colleague has not 
thought about risks, assign a poor rating.   

How to select a rating 
It is best to show a range of ratings.  Even the best performing nonprofits have room 
for improvement.  Even the worst performing nonprofits need something to feel good 
about.  Most questions require a judgement about your own nonprofit, not a 
comparison with others. If you feel uncomfortable, reach a group consensus.   

How accurate do I have to be? 
Unlike audited financial statements that require a high level of accuracy, these reports 
are for management purposes.  Stop when you feel that you have enough information 
to make a decision and that further analysis will not change that decision. 

Revenue Efficiency Report - How do I estimate the time staff spend on each 
donor type? 
Initially, an estimate from a supervisor is fine.  Since the data reports should be 
produced annually, consider improving how your marketing staff track their time 
going forward.   

What do I do if the data is not clean? 
If the data contradicts common sense, use common sense. 

Beware the “illusion of accuracy” 
Initially, staff time may be an estimate.  Initially, there may be noise in your database.  
Display results as words, not numbers, to avoid readers from getting hung up on the 
details or decimal points.  The point of the self-audit is to measure trends over time, 
not individual statistics.   

After the audit is done, what is next? 
Show your report to the Executive Director. Together decide on: 
•  Which staff receive your report and in which order.  Be sensitive to the fact that 

some employees can feel threatened by the results. 

•  How to reach group consensus on which areas to select for improvement next year.

title: Recruiting a NFP Board of Directors
content:
# Recruiting a NFP Board of Directors

Source: https://www.masadvise.org/mas-publications/

Board of Directors Recruitment Marketing

September 2019



































Step One: Advance Planning

Start by defining your needs
Finalize a role description
Clear expectations of the role
Develop a board application form
Identify the volunteers who will help with recruitment and the steps they will be involved with
Develop a recruitment package (mission, history, description, list of current board members, executive summary of your strategic plan, etc.)

Nb: consider maintaining a list of potential board candidates and their key skills moving forward



































Step Two: Make your organization more visible in your community

Your organization’s work in the community must be valued and generally understood beyond the present board and staff group to attract volunteers.  Ideas to make your organization more visible include:
Make presentations about your organization 
Ensure your website promotes the importance of what your organization does and the difference it makes in people’s lives.  
Use social media and e-newsletters to communicate externally what the board is currently working on 
Partner with like-minded businesses (they too have enews, websites, social platforms, etc.!)




Can you leverage your Media Relations?

1. Make a list of local media outlets and possibilities.Study all of the newspapers, even the free ones, in your area. Listen to radio stations and find out who does interviews on talk shows.
2. Get to know the interviewing style and interests of local reporters.Listen to talk radio and read the community newspaper with an eye to analyzing the slant and area of interest of various reporters. The more familiar you become with their work, the easier it will be to find a “hook” that will interest them in what your organization is doing.
3. Keep looking for opportunities that are appropriate to you.One day I noticed a tiny paragraph in the business section of our newspaper which said, “Have you left corporate life to start something on your own? If so, we’d like to hear from you for an upcoming story we’re doing about career changers.”  I promptly called the reporter’s voice mail, introduced myself and noted insights from those who move into the NFP sector.
Another of my favorite tools is a letter to the editor. If you see a story that deals with an area related to your business, your professional comments may be welcomed. You could write to applaud the original article or add additional information.

Are there opportunities during upcoming media interviews to make a note of the need to volunteers?
Treat media interviews like donor prospecting -  they can be seed planting expeditions and good will come from every effort sooner or later.
Consider – Why are we newsworthy?
Consider the subject-matter-expertise your team has and what types of interviews could provide positive media opportunities for your organization.
What impact has your organization had in the community recently?  What human interest stories would local readers be interested in?  What public service / educational opportunities exist?   What are the benefits of volunteering your volunteers receive? 

Media Assignment Desks

News desk - 640 Radio - newsroom@640toronto.com
News desk – 680 Radio – news680@rogers.com
Assignment editor - CP24 - breakingnews@cp24.com
Assignment editor - CBC Radio News English –tonews@cbc.ca
